questions.question: Why are Exact Match and token-F1 insufficient for evaluating modern LLM outputs?
options: They run too slowly at evaluation time, making them impractical for large test sets with many thousands of examples
They miss semantic equivalence entirely; 'June 29th, 2007' vs 'June 29, 2007' scores 0 EM despite being correct
They require a GPU to compute, unlike judge-based metrics which can run on CPU-only infrastructure
They are not differentiable, so they cannot be used as a training loss during fine-tuning
questions.explanation: Exact-match/F1 cannot recognize paraphrases or formatting differences that humans would mark correct.

questions.question: What does the RAGAS faithfulness metric measure?
options: Retrieval recall, the fraction of all relevant passages successfully returned by the retriever's top-K results
End-to-end latency, how long the full retrieval-plus-generation pipeline takes to return an answer
Raw generation throughput, measured in tokens produced per second during the answer-generation step
Whether each claim in the answer is entailed by the retrieved context, checked via an NLI entailment model
questions.explanation: Faithfulness checks each answer claim against retrieved context using NLI entailment.

questions.question: Why is judge-model calibration against human labels required before trusting scores?
options: If Spearman correlation between judge and human labels drops below roughly 0.7, the score is noise, not signal
It is a compliance requirement under the GDPR for any automated system that scores generated text
Calibrating the judge model against human labels measurably speeds up its inference latency
Calibration is fundamentally a tokenization issue caused by mismatched vocabularies between judge and generator
questions.explanation: Without calibration, you cannot tell whether judge scores reflect quality or model bias.

questions.question: What is self-evaluation bias in LLM-as-judge setups?
options: The claim that judge latency drops whenever the judge model shares a weights family with the generator
The observation that judges run measurably faster whenever they are scoring cached, previously seen model outputs
Using the same LLM family to both generate and judge inflates scores compared to using an independent judge model
The tendency of judge models to silently ignore any system prompt they are given during evaluation
questions.explanation: Same-family generator+judge biases scores upward; use a different model family for judging.

questions.question: What does G-Eval specifically add over a naive 'score 0-1' prompt?
options: A larger context window, letting the judge see substantially more of the full conversation history before scoring
Lower per-call cost, since G-Eval's structured format uses noticeably fewer tokens than a freeform prompt
An explicit chain-of-thought rubric that auto-expands into named evaluation steps, yielding more stable scores
Built-in multilingual scoring support that a plain 'score 0-1' prompt cannot provide on its own
questions.explanation: G-Eval's structured eval-steps produce more reliable scores than freeform 'rate it' prompts.

questions.question: Why is reporting only the aggregate mean score dangerous?
options: A 0.85 mean can hide a small tail of catastrophic failures; always inspect the bottom quantile of scores too
Aggregate numbers are simply too large in magnitude to fit cleanly into most CI/CD dashboards without truncation
Reporting an aggregate score silently discards the judge model's identity and version from the record
Computing the aggregate mean itself requires GPU resources that a CI pipeline may not have available
questions.explanation: Means hide tail failures; surface bottom-10% to catch high-severity issues.

questions.question: Why pin the judge model + version in CI?
options: It is a contractual requirement Anthropic imposes on anyone using its models as an evaluation judge
Pinning the judge model measurably lowers the per-call cost of running evaluation in CI pipelines
Unpinned judges are vulnerable to silent tokenizer drift, which corrupts the scoring input before evaluation even starts
Upgrading the judge model silently shifts every metric it produces; longitudinal comparison breaks without a frozen judge
questions.explanation: A judge upgrade silently shifts the metric baseline; pinning preserves cross-run comparability.

questions.question: Where does DeepEval fit relative to RAGAS?
options: DeepEval is a hosted-only SaaS product, unlike RAGAS which can only ever run as a self-hosted open-source library
DeepEval is pytest-for-LLMs (CI gates, G-Eval, hallucination metrics); RAGAS specializes in reference-free RAG monitoring
DeepEval is actually a tokenizer library, unrelated to LLM output evaluation or scoring at all
DeepEval fully replaces RAGAS, making RAGAS's four RAG-specific metrics obsolete for production use
questions.explanation: DeepEval anchors CI/CD regression testing; RAGAS handles reference-free RAG monitoring.
